passages.t: ‘Do not discard me in my old age’
passages.happening:
Psalm 71 has no heading. It opens with words close to the start of Psalm 31: “In You, O LORD, I have taken refuge; let me never be put to shame” (verse 1).

The one praying has trusted God all his life. “For You are my hope, O Lord GOD, my confidence from my youth. I have leaned on You since birth” (verses 5 and 6).

Now he is old, and afraid. “Do not discard me in my old age; do not forsake me when my strength fails” (verse 9). His enemies see a weak man and say, “God has forsaken him; pursue him and seize him, for there is no one to rescue him” (verse 11).

But he keeps hoping. “But I will always hope and will praise You more and more” (verse 14). And he has a purpose left. “Even when I am old and gray, do not forsake me, O God, until I proclaim Your power to the next generation” (verse 18). He expects God to lift him again: “Even from the depths of the earth You will bring me back up” (verse 20). The psalm ends with harp and lyre and praise “all day long” (verse 24).
passages.hearers:
Psalm 71 has no heading, which is rare in Book Two. Many readers take it as a prayer of the old David. Others think of an unnamed older worshipper, maybe a temple singer, since he promises to play the harp. The psalm does not say. It borrows lines from other psalms, especially Psalm 31 and Psalm 22: “Be not far from me” (verse 12) echoes Psalm 22:11.

Israel's law said, “You are to rise in the presence of the elderly, honor the aged” (Leviticus 19:32). But when strength failed, old people depended on family and neighbours. If they had none, they were easy targets. The taunt of verse 11 says what people often assumed: if an old man is weak and alone, God must have dropped him.

‘A portent to many’ (verse 7) may mean that people pointed at his troubles as a sign of God's anger. Or it may mean that his long life with God was itself a sign.
passages.later:
God promised through Isaiah, “Even to your old age, I will be the same, and I will bear you up when you turn gray” (Isaiah 46:4).

Luke tells of Anna, a widow of eighty-four, who “worshiped night and day” and was one of the first to speak of the child Jesus (Luke 2:37-38). Paul writes, “Though our outer self is wasting away, yet our inner self is being renewed day by day” (2 Corinthians 4:16).

The taunt ‘God has forsaken him’ was thrown at Jesus on the cross: “Let God deliver Him now if He wants Him” (Matthew 27:43).
passages.asks:
If you are old, this psalm is your prayer. You are allowed to be afraid of weakness and of being set aside. Say verse 9 to God. And notice verse 18: you still have work to do. Someone younger needs to hear what God has done in your long life.

If you care for someone old, this psalm asks you to be part of God's answer to verse 9. An old person should never be left to feel ‘there is no one to rescue him’. Visit, listen, and ask them about the God of their youth.

If the weakness of age has brought you low in spirit, you do not have to carry that alone. Tell someone you trust, a family member, a pastor or a doctor.
